paper_title: Gluing Local Contexts into Global Meaning: A Sheaf-Theoretic Decomposition of Transformer Representations

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Existing interpretability tools do not test whether a representation keeps the same content when only the phrasing changes. We treat each paraphrase pair as a local witness that two activations should agree and build a cellular sheaf over the paraphrase graph; its Laplacian $L_\mathcal{F}$ answers the question on a frozen model with no training. The kernel $H^0$ is a content subspace: at 20 dimensions it beats the preserved subspace of the concept eraser LEACE on held-out CounterFact fact retrieval across eight architectures by a mean $+17.1$\,pp, and constraining all paraphrases of a fact jointly adds a further $+6.5$\,pp. The spectral complement concentrates causal influence: ablating the most paraphrase-variable coordinates, a coordinate-wise proxy for it, changes model outputs $5.6$ to $26.5\times$ more than ablating coordinates of matched per-coordinate variability, across nine models from 124M to 13B parameters. Stacking layers into a grid creates $b_1 = N(L-1)$ algebraic 1-cycles, and the resulting model-derived harmonic mass varies by nearly three orders of magnitude across six architectures and ranks them as their steering fragility does (Spearman $ρ= 0.90$, exact one-sided permutation $p = 0.014$). The same paraphrase graph yields the content subspace, the influence directions, and the fragility measure. Project page: https://cwru-aism.github.io/gluing-lc-page/

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Transformer representations entangle what sentence means with how it is phrased. The hidden state for The Eiffel Tower is in Paris differs from Paris is home to the Eiffel Tower despite identical semantic content. Existing tools decompose one activation into features [7, 12], test the linear decodability of attributes already chosen [4], or relate two activation spaces to each other [40, 52]. None of them tests cross-context consistency, meaning whether feature encodes the same information when the phrasing changes and the meaning does not. The gap shows up in steering, where methods improve some models and fail or degrade others [14], and even within one model steerability varies widely across inputs [57]; no existing tool predicts which regime model is in. We treat the problem as local-to-global agreement. Each paraphrase pair is local witness that two activations should agree, and together the witnesses should determine one global answer. In the cellular sheaf we build on the paraphrase graph, hidden states sit on the nodes, edges connect paraphrase pairs, and learned restriction map (P Rdk) projects each pair into shared k-dimensional comparison space. The coboundary δ0 measures pairwise disagreement, and the sheaf Laplacian LF = (δ0)δ0 has kernel 0 = ker(δ0) of globally consistent sections together with spectral complement of high-disagreement directions. We call the spectral complement the 1 directions (Remark 3.3 explains the name). Section 3 defines the construction, and Section 5 tests it on nine models. 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Figure 1: Sheaf decomposition of paraphrase pair. It carries b1 = (L 1) algebraic 1-cycles (b1, the first Betti number, counts the independent cycles in the graph), one per elementary square, and each square asks whether the layer-l-to-layer-l+1 transformation commutes with paraphrase equivalence. The model-derived Hodge harmonic mass (the fraction of model-derived edge cochains energy in the harmonic subspace, the part supported on cycles that is neither gradient nor curl) at = 2 varies by nearly three orders of magnitude across six architectures (104 to 0.08; Table 1) against 0.25 topological reference, and 5.4 tests it as diagnostic of steering fragility. sections.title: 5.1 Setup and Datasets
sections.content: We evaluate on nine transformer models spanning architecture families (GPT-2 [51], Llama [59, 26], Mistral [38], Qwen [65], phi [42], Gemma [24], OLMo [49]) and scales (124M to 13B parameters). Functional validation ablates coordinates on 1000 sentences (four models; 666 MRPC and 334 PAWS) or 100 MRPC sentences (five models). Restriction maps (PCA, CCA, contrastive Fisher) are learned from 200 pairs of the Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus (MRPC) [16]. Steering uses the CounterFact benchmark [47] (n = 1000 per model), and fact retrieval uses ROME CounterFact: 500 facts split 70/30 for the held-out comparison (5.2), with 60-fact, 5-paraphrase subset for the topology constructions. We extract mean-pooled hidden states at layer ℓ 2L/3, set edge dimension = 128 (capturing 98% paired variance), take the bottom and top 20 eigenvectors as 0 and 1 directions, and norm-match all steering vectors to α = 0.3h. Bootstrap CIs use 1000 resamples, McNemars test [46] handles paired comparisons, and Cohens [11] reports effect sizes.

Fragility is the fraction of CounterFact facts preserved under random direction norm-matched to 0.3 times the hidden-state norm at layer 5L/8 (Appendix A.3). The three lowest-mass architectures are the three most robust and the three highest are the three most fragile: Spearman ρ = 0.90, exact one-sided permutation = 0.014 over the 720 rankings. The one rank inversion, Qwen-2.5-7B against Llama-3-8B, is within sampling error (34.3% vs. 36.0%). Table 1 lists both quantities per model. Style change is measured as the fraction of outputs differing from baseline, and fact preservation is the fraction containing the target entity (greedy decoding, 50 tokens). sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: This paper extends non-archival workshop version [25] that contained only the single-layer construction with three pilot experiments; the multi-layer grids, relation hypergraphs (b1 = 66), harmonicmass fragility diagnostic, held-out LEACE protocol, restriction-map ablation, PIXEL comparison, baseline suite, and self-supervised learning (SSL) connection are new. 9 Sheaves in machine learning. Hansen and Ghrist [31] developed the spectral theory of the sheaf Laplacian, which specializes to the connection Laplacian of Singer and Wu [56] on O(d)-bundles, and Hansen and Gebhart [29] introduced sheaf neural networks, since applied to heterophilic graphs [6, 2, 34], predictive coding [55], and restriction-map learning [15]. Duta et al. [17] build sheaf hypergraph networks, and Mule et al. [48] unify directed/undirected hypergraph Laplacians. In the closest concurrent work on transformers, Krasnovsky [41] proposes sheaf-inconsistency score for circuit coherence and Javidnia [37] builds context-chart atlases with Fisher metrics and holonomy. We differ in stalks (paraphrase-graph nodes carrying hidden states under PCA/CCA/contrastive restrictions) and in target (post-hoc 0/H 1 decomposition for retrieval and steering). Subspace interpretability. Sparse autoencoders [7, 12, 58, 20], probes [4], causal abstraction [22], CKA/SVCCA [40, 52], and distributed alignment search (DAS) and LEACE [23, 5] target individual features or whole-space comparison. The log det Cov regulariser of 7 shares its geometry with the decorrelation terms of VICReg [3] and Barlow Twins [67]. Invariance objectives (contrastive: SimCLR [9], InfoNCE [61]; non-contrastive: BYOL [27], Barlow Twins [67]; DCCA [1]) are training-time analogues that achieve paired-view agreement during training, while we read invariance off frozen model via ker(LF ). Steering and linear representations. Activation addition [60], representation engineering [69], and their variants [66, 63, 39] inject directions and are compared in unified evaluation by Im and Li [35], while Da Silva et al. [14] document model-dependent steering reliability across 36 models and Tan et al. [57] document input-level unreliability, which 5.4 relates to harmonic mass. The linear-representation hypothesis [50, 28, 33] is qualified by Engels et al. [19] and Makelov et al. [45]; our coordinate ablations use per-coordinate variability-matched controls, which address that concern only in part (5.3). We compare empirically to PIXEL (5.4, Appendix B.11); Angular Steering [63] and MSRS [35] are application-side and orthogonal.

sections.title: 7 Discussion
sections.content: Proposition 3.1 reduces LF to projected covariance for single shared with identity transports, here on the matching graph. Within that regime the restriction-map ablation locates content in the kernel of the within-pair difference covariance  (Table 11)  , and joint multi-paraphrase constraints add +6.5 pp (Appendix B.3). Beyond it, multi-layer grids carry model-derived harmonic mass whose ranking tracks steering fragility (5.4). The mass needs only 30 MRPC pairs and one forward pass per sentence, so it can screen model before steering sweep. Graphs that join activations of different dimension (text and image encoders, or models of different width) need per-node maps Pv of different widths, which we leave to future work. Self-supervised connection. sheaf-regularized objective = tr(LF ) β log det Cov(f ) pairs VICRegs invariance term (tr LF is the within-pair MSE up to scale) with log-determinant spread term that, like VICRegs variance and covariance terms [3] and Barlow Twins redundancy reduction [67], penalizes dimensional collapse, though not in VICRegs hinge-plus-off-diagonal form; such regularizers are used alongside non-contrastive objectives such as BYOL and SimSiam [27, 10]. Across seven architectures the regulariser holds encoder rank at 5760/64 where naive MSE collapses to 1442/64 (per-architecture breakdown in Appendix B.14). Limitations. is architectureand partially domain-dependent (Appendix B.1); operating regime is α [0.10, 0.15]; node-space 1 does not transfer and cycle holonomy does not differ significantly from shuffled null (Appendices B.13, B.12); the fragility diagnostic is rank correlation over six architectures (ρ = 0.90), and more architectures are needed before it serves as predictor. The construction needs only grouping of contexts asserted to be equivalent, and cross-lingual probe (Appendix B.8) shows it transfers to translation pairs; logical equivalence and dialogue continuation fit the same template but are untested.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: We framed cross-context consistency as sheaf condition: paraphrase pairs are local witnesses of agreement, the kernel of the sheaf Laplacian glues them into content subspace, and its spectral complement holds the phrasing-dependent variation, all read off frozen model without training. The kernel beats the preserved subspace of LEACE on held-out retrieval, the spectral complement 10 concentrates causal influence, and the cycles the same operator exposes across layers give harmonic mass whose ranking tracks steering fragility across six architectures (ρ = 0.90).

sections.content: A.1 Algebraic 1 = 0 on Richer Topologies 26 27 28 28 On the matching graph used in the main paper, 1 = 0 algebraically because the graph is acyclic and is surjective. To produce topology with 1 = 0, we construct three complexes from the same 300 activation vectors (60 facts, 5 paraphrases each): 1. Matching graph (paper baseline): 300 nodes, 120 edges (one per paraphrase pair), 0 faces. Algebraic 1 = 0. 2. Fact clique (filled): 300 nodes, 600 edges (all pairs), 600 filled triangles. Each clique is simply connected, so 1 = 0 (though 2 = 240). 3. PIXEL exhibits the same architecture-dependent fragility pattern documented for our methods: it strongly improves over CAA on fragile Llama-2-7B but gets approached or beaten by random on robust Mistral-7B. This supports the architecture-diagnostic interpretation: the influenceconcentration mechanism (5.4) is shared across direction-extraction recipes. PIXELs dual-view direction extraction is stronger choice than CAAs mean-of-differences, but the closed-form perposition calibration does not overcome architecture fragility. Contrastive sheaf steering with the architecture-matched restriction map remains the strongest single method on Llama-2-7B (31.0%); CCA sheaf steering is strongest on Mistral-7B (41.6%); no sheaf method beats random on Llama-3-8B at α = 0.30. What we did not implement: PIXELs per-question soft-gating uses labeled MC2 score on TruthfulQA, which CounterFact does not expose; we use single global direction. PIXELs continuationposition injection (the include-pred option) requires modifying activations during incremental decoding with KV cache, which would constitute larger surgery than the direction-vs-direction comparison we want here. PIXELs residual_scale and auto-flip are tuned per benchmark in their paper; we keep both at default (1.0, no flip) and rely on sign-aligned PCA. Sheaf construction (restriction map + Laplacian) takes < 1 minute per model; dominant cost is activation extraction (identical to any activation-based method). Hyperparameters: Edge dimension = 128 (capturing 98% of variance). Mean pooling over sequence positions. Restriction map learned via joint PCA. Top/bottom 20 eigenvectors define 0/H 1. Steering vectors norm-matched to 30% of mean hidden state norm. Layer selection: retrieval and the sheaf constructions use ℓ = 0.67L (layer 8 for GPT-2, layer 21 for 32-layer models), and steering uses ℓ = 5L/8 (layer 7 for GPT-2, layer 20 for 32-layer models). Targets middle-to-late layers where semantic content is well-formed but output projections have not dominated. Statistical tests: Bootstrap confidence intervals (1000 resamples). Mann-Whitney for group comparisons. McNemar for paired binary outcomes. Cohens (continuous) and Cohens (proportions) for effect sizes. All p-values are two-sided except the Spearman and holonomy permutation tests, which are exact one-sided in the pre-specified direction. 27 C.3 Practitioner Guidance Recommended workflow: (1) Build the sheaf with 200+ MRPC paraphrase pairs using PCA restriction maps (parameter-free default). (2) Apply steering at moderate α (0.100.15) using both 1 dims and 0-removed, selecting the best on validation set (n=50). (3) For fragile models (identifiable via single random-steering probe), use sheaf 1 to avoid generation collapse. For robust models, expect random steering to be competitive at α 0.30; prefer moderate magnitudes for sheaf advantage. C.4 NeurIPS Paper Checklist 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the papers contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Section 1 enumerates three contributions, with the SSL result reported in 7: (i) 0 beats LEACE on held-out CounterFact, the kernel selection carries the result under random or identity , and joint multi-paraphrase constraints add +6.5 pp (Tables 2, 11, 10); (ii) 1 functional influence (5.626.5 over coordinates of matched per-coordinate variability; Table 3); (iii) multi-layer grids carry harmonic mass that ranks six architectures by steering fragility at ρ = 0.90 (Table 1, Appendix A.3). Each claim is supported by experiments in 5 with effect sizes, p-values, and bootstrap CIs. The negative result on MLST cycle/transition terms is reported in Appendix B.15  (Table 18)  . 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Section 7 contains an explicit Limitations paragraph covering: (a) restrictionmap selection is architecture-dependent (contrastive Fisher wins on Llama-2-7B, CCA on Mistral-7B); (b) restriction-map selection is partially domain-dependent (cross-corpus costs 25 pp, Appendix B.1); (c) sheaf steering wins at α [0.10, 0.15] but ties random at α = 0.30 on robust models; (d) node-space operationalization of relation-hypergraph 1 did not transfer to retrieval (Appendix B.13); (e) cycle holonomy does not differ significantly from shuffled-paraphrase null (Appendix B.12); (f) the MLST cycle/transition terms are neutral-to-slightly-negative as training signal (Appendix B.15); (g) our PIXEL comparison uses simplified port (single global direction; Appendix B.11); we do not empirically compare to Angular Steering or MSRS (orthogonal frameworks). 3. Theory, Assumptions and Proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper has one Proposition (Proposition 3.1: reduction of the sheaf Laplacian to projected within-pair covariance). The assumptions are stated explicitly in the proposition body (shared-projection matching-graph regime, one for every node, Quv = on edges); the failure regime under per-node Pv and Procrustes transports is also stated. The full proof is provided in Appendix A.5. Remark 3.3 clarifies the algebraic-vs-spectral 1 distinction so the cohomological language is unambiguous. 4. Experimental Result Reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The pipeline is specified in equation form in 3 (joint-PCA restriction map, sheaf Laplacian as projected within-pair covariance, 0/H 1 as smallest/largest eigenspaces, mean-difference steering with 0-removal). All hyperparameters (edge dimension = 128, 0/H 1 count = 20, layer ℓ 2L/3 (5L/8 for steering), steering norm α = 0.3h, MLP encoder geometry 256 256 64, training step counts) are documented in 5 and Appendix C.2. Datasets are public (MRPC, PAWS, QQP, STS-B, CounterFact) with standard splits and 70/30 train/test for the LEACE comparison. Quantization (4-bit bitsandbytes for 7B+ models) and layer selection rules are explicit. 28 5. Open Access to Data and Code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes] Justification: All datasets used are public benchmarks with standard licenses (cited in 5 and below). Code implementing the sheaf decomposition, steering pipeline, multilayer grid, and MLST, with claim-by-claim reproduction guide, is released at https: //github.com/CWRU-AISM/gluing-lc. The construction in 3 together with the hyperparameters in Appendix C.2 is sufficient to reimplement the pipeline from the paper alone, and all numerical results are deterministic given the published hyperparameters and seeds. 6. Experimental Setting/Details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer, etc.) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Section 5 (Setup and Datasets) and Appendix C.2 specify: nine architectures with sizes; layer selection rule ℓ 2L/3 (5L/8 for steering); edge dimension = 128 chosen to capture 98% paired variance; 0/H 1 slice = 20; bootstrap CIs with 1000 resamples; McNemars test for paired comparisons; restriction maps (PCA / CCA / contrastive Fisher) and how each is fit; 200 MRPC pairs for sheaf construction; CounterFact = 1000 for steering; 70/30 fact split for LEACE comparison. 7. Experiment Statistical Significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Bootstrap 95% CIs are reported alongside every steering and retrieval point estimate (Tables 3, 4, 2). McNemars exact test is used for paired binary outcomes; Cohens for effect sizes; MannWhitney for unpaired comparisons. Multiple-comparisons control via BenjaminiHochberg is detailed in Appendix B.10. MLST results are over ten seeds with reported standard deviations and paired t-tests. All p-values are two-sided except the Spearman and holonomy permutation tests, which are exact one-sided in the pre-specified direction. 8. Experiments Compute Resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Appendix C.2 reports hardware (NVIDIA A100 80GB or RTX 4090 24GB), 4-bit quantization for 7B+ models, and execution time (sheaf construction < 1 minute per model; activation extraction is the dominant cost). Total project compute is approximately 200 GPU-hours. Section 5 indicates the cluster setup; no experiment requires more than single A100. 9. Code of Ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The work is interpretability research on publicly released language models using public paraphrase and factual-recall benchmarks. No human subjects, no crowdsourcing, no scraping of private data, no release of new high-risk artifacts. Datasets used (MRPC, PAWS, QQP, STS-B, CounterFact) are standard licensed benchmarks. We have read the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and conform. 10. Broader Impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The work is interpretability research aimed at improving transparency of large language model representations. Positive impact: label-free decomposition that exposes which directions in residual streams are content-stable across paraphrasing and which carry surface variation, potentially aiding red-teaming, alignment audits, and the diagnosis of model fragility (the steering analysis in 5.4 is itself fragility diagnostic). Negative impact: the same machinery could in principle be used to construct targeted style or stance interventions against safety guardrails. We frame steering as diagnostic tool rather than deployment mechanism, and we report architecture-dependent failure modes (random steering can outperform sheaf steering at α = 0.30 on robust models, which curbs naive misuse). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have high risk for misuse (e.g., pretrained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [NA] Justification: The paper does not release new pretrained models, generative models, or scraped datasets. We analyze existing publicly released language models (GPT-2, Llama-2/3, Mistral, Qwen, phi-2, Gemma, OLMo) using existing public benchmarks. The released artifact is analysis code, not model checkpoint or dataset. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: All datasets and models are cited at first use: MRPC [16], PAWS [68], QQP [36], CounterFact [47], TruthfulQA [44]. Models are accessed through their official Hugging Face releases under their respective licenses (Apache-2.0 for Mistral and Qwen; the Llama-2/3 community license; MIT for phi-2; Apache-2.0 for OLMo; Gemma terms of use; MIT for GPT-2). Each is used within the terms permitted for academic research. 13. New Assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [NA] Justification: The paper introduces no new datasets, no new pretrained models, and no new benchmarks. All releasable artifacts are analysis code; the code repository documents them with claim-by-claim reproduction guide. 14. Crowdsourcing and Research with Human Subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Answer: [NA] Justification: The paper involves no crowdsourcing and no human subjects. All evaluation is automated against public benchmarks. 15. Institutional Review Board (IRB) Approvals or Equivalent for Research with Human Subjects Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained? Answer: [NA] Justification: No human subjects are involved; no IRB approval is required. 16. Declaration of LLM Usage Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigorousness, or originality of the research, declaration is not required. Answer: [NA] Justification: The paper analyzes pretrained LLMs (GPT-2, Llama-2/3, Mistral, Qwen, phi2, Gemma, OLMo) as objects of study; it does not use LLMs as part of its core methodology 30 to generate science content, design the cohomological framework, derive the proposition, or run the experiments. Any LLM-assisted writing or editing is non-substantive and does not change methodology, rigor, or originality.
